questions.q: What replaces T-SQL's TOP for limiting rows in Snowflake?
questions.explain: Snowflake has no TOP keyword; it uses LIMIT, the same keyword PostgreSQL and MySQL use.

questions.q: What operator does Snowflake use for string concatenation, replacing T-SQL's +?
options: CONCAT() only, with no operator form
questions.explain: Snowflake uses the ANSI-standard || operator for concatenation instead of T-SQL's overloaded +.

questions.q: How does Snowflake handle unquoted identifier case, and which other dialect does this resemble?
options: Case-sensitive by default, like PostgreSQL's quoted identifiers
Case-insensitive, folded to UPPERCASE internally — the same family of behavior as Oracle
Snowflake requires all identifiers to be quoted
Case-insensitive but preserves exact typed case, like T-SQL
questions.explain: Unquoted Snowflake identifiers are case-insensitive and folded to UPPERCASE internally, the same family of behavior as Oracle; quoting preserves exact case and makes the identifier case-sensitive.

questions.q: What does Snowflake's QUALIFY clause let you avoid writing?
options: A wrapping CTE or subquery just to filter on a window function's result
questions.explain: QUALIFY filters directly on a window function's output (e.g. ROW_NUMBER() = 1) without needing to wrap the query in a CTE or subquery first, unlike T-SQL.

questions.q: What does Snowflake's Time Travel feature (AT / BEFORE clauses) let you do?
options: Roll back a transaction after it commits
Schedule a query to run at a future time
Query a table as it existed at a past point in time
Automatically archive old rows to cold storage
questions.explain: Time Travel lets you query historical data using AT or BEFORE clauses (by offset or timestamp) — a genuine Snowflake-specific feature with no T-SQL equivalent.
